author_final_remarks.value:
Dear Area Chair,

We sincerely appreciate the efforts and valuable feedback provided by the AC and the reviewers. Below is our final remark.

First of all, we thank the reviewers for recognizing our work. All reviewers recommended acceptance in their initial opinions (three Accept and one Borderline Accept). Notably, the reviewer with Borderline Accept is considering raising the score further. As highlighted in the Strengths of the review opinions, the main contributions of our benchmark can be summarized as follows: 1) It offers broad evaluation coverage with 23 text-centric tasks across 31 text-rich scenarios; 2) It contains 10,000 high-quality human-verified QA pairs; 3) It includes a private test set to ensure rigorous evaluation; 4) It enables a holistic evaluation on 8 core OCR competencies; 5) It provides in-depth analysis of current LMM limitations.

Furthermore, we have comprehensively addressed all reviewer concerns in our rebuttal, and no new objections were proposed. After the Discussion period, all reviewers either increased their scores or maintained their original Accept decisions. The main points for our rebuttal are as follows:
1. Reviewer 7Ywt questioned the necessity of including reasoning tasks and the weighting of different tasks. We explained the evolution of OCR tasks, the impact of prior unified benchmarks, and the community expectations. The reviewer agrees with our perspective and considers further raising the score (initial score is Borderline Accept).
2. Reviewer pBxC raised concerns about the potential data contamination and biases in data construction. In the rebuttal, we clarified the use of private data and gave more details on bias control, leading the reviewer to maintain the Accept decision.
3. Reviewer kPeC suggested deeper analyses of failure cases. We addressed this by offering more thorough discussions of common LMM limitations.
4. Reviewer Zfje asked about the exclusion of multi-image tasks and requested documentation of the annotation protocol. In our rebuttal, we explained the rationale for focusing on single-image evaluation and provided details of our annotation procedures.

In summary, thanks again for the positive evaluations from all reviewers! The suggestions in the review opinions help further improve our paper, while they don’t affect the contributions of our work. As demonstrated in the rebuttal and discussion stages, all reviewer concerns have been resolved. We hope this is helpful for your assessment.

> **Comments: 1. I believe there is an issue with the paper. Although it covers many text-related tasks, for example, the Mathematical Reasoning task in Figure 1 actually resembles more of a Visual Math Reasoning problem, with the only difference being that the question is converted into optical characters. Is it really necessary to include such tasks in OCRBench? Similarly, the Reasoning VQA maze task in Figure 3 should not be a focus of OCRBench. It is more about evaluating the model’s logical reasoning ability. If the authors intend to include it in their benchmark, they should differentiate whether the model's failure is due to incorrect character recognition or a lack of reasoning capability, which would align better with OCRBench's purpose. Otherwise, the resulting scores and rankings may not truly reflect the OCR capabilities of the models and could mislead many in the community. 2. As a benchmark, the weighted scores across different tasks significantly affect the model's performance in the average. The paper does not seem to discuss the weights of its 23 tasks, nor which tasks accurately reflect real-world application needs and fundamental OCR abilities. Providing feedback on a model’s foundational OCR capabilities and its ability to solve practical problems is what a benchmark should focus on. This would have a more positive impact on the community, rather than getting caught up in an "arms race" to cover a wide range of tasks and pile on more features.**

We sincerely appreciate your insightful comments. We understand your concern regarding the inclusion of reasoning-heavy tasks. While these tasks may appear to extend beyond conventional OCR boundaries, we believe they are essential to holistically evaluating modern OCR systems, especially in the context of large multimodal models (LMMs). We offer the following justifications:

**1. OCR is no longer just about recognition. Modern tasks demand understanding and reasoning.**
OCR capabilities have seen significant progress, with many LMMs now excelling at end-to-end performance across diverse tasks. Modern OCR goes beyond basic character recognition—real-world documents often involve complex layouts and semantic structures that demand contextual understanding and reasoning. OCRBench v2 is designed to reflect this evolution, aligning its evaluation with the actual demands of contemporary OCR applications.

Importantly, modern LMMs no longer follow a strict “recognize-then-reason” pipeline. Instead, recognition and reasoning can be treated as parallel visual question-answering tasks, such as “What does the text say?” and “What can be inferred from the visual text?” This reframing treats both as co-equal competencies rather than sequential steps. If a model accurately answers a reasoning question grounded in visual text, it implicitly demonstrates robust recognition and comprehension. Conversely, strong text recognition often reflects effective visual-linguistic inference from noisy or visual structured inputs.

**2. Broader evaluation design is in line with precedent from other influential benchmarks.**
Several recent benchmarks have embraced integrated evaluation frameworks. For example, XLRS-Bench [1] includes spatial and logical reasoning tasks, such as path planning, to assess visual navigation, not just perception. More notably, the Visual Question Answering (VQA) benchmark has, for over a decade, assessed models end-to-end based on final answers, without requiring intermediate evaluations like explicit detection or parsing. While such intermediate evaluation can be valuable in some settings, the enduring success of VQA demonstrates the value of holistic, task-level assessment. It has driven real progress across both vision and language communities. In the same spirit, OCRBench v2 aims to evaluate OCR systems in terms of what ultimately matters: can a model understand and reason over visual text to produce correct and meaningful answers?

Regarding the weighted scores across tasks, while we acknowledge that task importance may vary across applications, we argue that introducing explicit weights for each of the 23 tasks might not always be beneficial. Task-level weighting often involves subjective choices and may introduce bias, whereas our current approach (aggregating scores across all instructions) naturally reflects task significance through coverage: tasks with broader scenarios include more instructions and thus contribute more to the overall score. This instruction-level averaging avoids arbitrary weighting, ensures fair treatment of all instances, and encourages general-purpose model development rather than task-specific tuning. In addition, previous influential benchmarks, such as MME[2], MMCOMPOSITION[3], and HALLUSIONBENCH[4] use similar approaches. Specifically, while MME calculates the overall score by summing the results from all instruction samples, the rest compute the average score across all subtasks. Moreover, our benchmark is modular and extensible: users can customize weights or focus on subsets using the provided metadata. Therefore, we argue that the equal instruction-level weighting can offer a balanced, reproducible, and flexible evaluation framework.

**3. Alignment with the community’s evolving expectations.**
As also noted by Reviewer pBxC, our benchmark “provides a thorough evaluation framework encapsulating fundamental and advanced text-centric challenges.” This reflects a growing recognition in the research community that text-rich visual reasoning tasks are not peripheral, but increasingly essential to OCR evaluation in the LMM era. After all, if a system were expected to perform only pure OCR, there would be little need to involve LMMs at all. As OCR systems evolve from isolated recognition modules into general-purpose visual-language understanding agents, evaluation protocols must evolve in parallel to remain meaningful.


In response to your concern, we have included a follow-up experiment to analyze whether reasoning errors stem from recognition failures. Our findings show that: some incorrect reasoning cases do result from recognition errors, while others occur despite correct recognition. There are also cases where the model misreads part of the text but still answers the reasoning question correctly. For example, in one task, the image shows the sentence: “Lily has 4 apples. She buys 3 more. How many apples does she have now?” The model mistakenly reads the “4” as “1” in the OCR step. But it still answers “7”—likely because it sees a picture of 4 apples next to the text. This shows that even when the OCR result is incorrect, the model can sometimes rely on visual cues from the image to reason correctly. It also demonstrates that recognition and reasoning are not strictly separate—they can support each other. 

Therefore, from the evolving capabilities of LMMs to the expanding scope of OCR tasks and the growing demand for comprehensive evaluation, we believe a direct benchmark is both timely and meaningful to reflect how OCR is truly practiced today in the era of LMMs.

[1] Wang F, Wang H, Guo Z, et al. Xlrs-bench: Could your multimodal llms understand extremely large ultra-high-resolution remote sensing imagery?[C]//Proceedings of the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference. 2025: 14325-14336.

[2]Yin, Shukang, Chaoyou Fu, Sirui Zhao, Ke Li, Xing Sun, Tong Xu, and Enhong Chen. "A survey on multimodal large language models." National Science Review 11, no. 12 (2024): nwae403.

[3]Hua, Hang, Yunlong Tang, Ziyun Zeng, Liangliang Cao, Zhengyuan Yang, Hangfeng He, Chenliang Xu, and Jiebo Luo. "Mmcomposition: Revisiting the compositionality of pre-trained vision-language models." arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.09733 (2024).

[4]Guan, Tianrui, Fuxiao Liu, Xiyang Wu, Ruiqi Xian, Zongxia Li, Xiaoyu Liu, Xijun Wang et al. > **Q1: The reviewer suggests the authors have some private data to evaluate some specific abilities of the models. The reviewer also has some concerns regarding the data contamination. How can the authors make sure the testing data does not overlap with the training data?**

Thanks for your suggestions! We have indeed constructed the private data to address this issue.

As stated in Lines 150-159, the private test set comprises 1,500 manually collected, text-rich images with human-annotated labels. Among the private data, 735 images were manually captured, and 765 images were sourced from unlabeled data with diverse scenarios. 

Although it is difficult to fully trace or verify whether some publicly available images have been seen during the training of LMMs, we ensure that all our instruction formulations and annotations are entirely private and won't be released publicly. Therefore, from a data construction perspective, the benchmark is designed to be unseen by current models.

In addition, the following tables exhibit the performance of the top 20 LMMs we have tested so far on our private test set, and we will update this result every quarter. We can observe a certain degree of consistency in performance trends and model rankings across public and private test sets. This suggests that there is no significant overlap between the public test set and the training data to some degree. Furthermore, our reserved private data can help to minimize the risk of data contamination.

> **Q1: The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of specific cases where multiple LMMs consistently fail, limiting insights into common failure modes across models.**

Thank you for your comments! Below are our in-depth analyses for common limitations of LMMs, including rare text recognition and fine-grained spatial perception.

Firstly, **rare text recognition** remains a challenge for LMMs, especially when dealing with less common formats, such as dot matrix text and mathematical symbols. To further investigate this, we classify occluded text, CAPTCHA, and dot-matrix text as low-frequency text, while other types are categorized as high-frequency text. We then conduct recognition experiments on both categories using LMMs. Notably, recognition accuracy varies significantly across these categories. The table below shows the performance of some LMMs on high-frequency and low-frequency texts.

#### LMMs' performance on high- and low-frequency words
| Category | Pixtral-12B | Cambrian-8B | InternVL2.5-8B | InternVL3-14B  | Qwen2.5VL-7B |
|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| High Frequency | 58.3 | 59.8 |  59.2  |   79.1  |   84.5  |
| Low Frequency | 23.6 | 40.2 |  28.1  |   46.7  |   53.3  |

Secondly, **fine-grained spatial perception** is another limitation for current LMMs, as indicated by the low performance of tasks requiring precise spatial understanding, such as text referring and text spotting. For instance, when provided with coordinate information as input, many models are able to output the relevant content from captions or chapters. However, almost all models struggle to accurately retrieve the corresponding text from documents with dense text based on given coordinates. In addition, LMMs have difficulty precisely predicting the coordinates corresponding to the given question. For instance, we investigate the content response accuracy and the IoU score for answer region localization in the VQA with position task. The table below suggests that although LMMs can roughly identify where the answer is located, they struggle to output the exact region.

> **Q1: The benchmark's design deliberately focuses only on single-image text-related scenarios. While the authors justify this as a focus on a fundamental problem, it omits the challenge of multi-page or multi-image document understanding, which is a critical aspect of many real-world applications.**

Thank you for this insightful comment! We fully acknowledge that multi-image or multi-page document understanding is an important and emerging research direction. However, our benchmark deliberately focuses on single-image scenarios for the following reasons:

First, single-image understanding remains a fundamental and unsolved challenge. Many leading LMMs still struggle with diverse single-image tasks, especially those involving complex layout, reasoning, or low-quality inputs. Our goal is to address these core issues before extending to more complex setups.

Second, multi-image scenarios often require dedicated architectural support, such as inter-image context modeling, memory handling, or hierarchical attention. These capabilities are not yet standard across many popular LMMs (e.g., Cambrian [1], Molmo [2]), and supporting them would limit the benchmark’s inclusiveness.

Third, the technical challenges and application goals of multi-image tasks differ significantly from those in single-image tasks. For instance, long-document understanding benchmarks like MMLONGBENCH-DOC [3] emphasize long-context modeling rather than fine-grained visual-text alignment in a single view.

Therefore, while multi-image tasks are undoubtedly important, we believe they represent a distinct frontier requiring separate benchmarks and modeling strategies. As the field advances, the distinction between single-image and multi-image understanding in multimodal models may gradually diminish, and a unified evaluation of both may become more appropriate. Thank you again for your valuable suggestion!

[1] Tong, Peter, Ellis Brown, Penghao Wu, Sanghyun Woo, Adithya Jairam Vedagiri IYER, Sai Charitha Akula, Shusheng Yang et al. "Cambrian-1: A fully open, vision-centric exploration of multimodal llms." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (2024): 87310-87356.

[2] Deitke, Matt, Christopher Clark, Sangho Lee, Rohun Tripathi, Yue Yang, Jae Sung Park, Mohammadreza Salehi et al. "Molmo and pixmo: Open weights and open data for state-of-the-art multimodal models." arXiv e-prints (2024): arXiv-2409.

[3] Ma, Yubo, Yuhang Zang, Liangyu Chen, Meiqi Chen, Yizhu Jiao, Xinze Li, Xinyuan Lu et al. "Mmlongbench-doc: Benchmarking long-context document understanding with visualizations." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (2024): 95963-96010.

> **Q2: The paper mentions that the benchmark construction involved human filtering and annotation, but it lacks detailed documentation regarding the specific annotation protocols, inter-annotator agreement statistics, or how ambiguous cases were resolved.**

Thanks! Our data annotation process is described as follows:

Before starting the annotation, we conducted thorough discussions to establish clear and consistent guidelines. For example, in questions involving numbers such as dates, amounts, or frequencies, answers were required to include all common formats—Arabic numerals, English abbreviations, and full English expressions. For coordinate-related questions, all coordinate values in the answers were normalized to a 0–1000 scale based on the image size to ensure consistency across varying image resolutions. In cases where multiple correct answers were possible, all valid answers were included. For the ``read all text'' task, we required that the answer follow a natural reading order from left to right and from top to bottom.

Based on these guidelines, 15 professional annotators carried out the annotation work. Each annotator strictly adhered to the instructions and created QA pairs along with the relevant coordinate information, depending on the task requirements.

After the initial annotation, we performed a manual cross-validation process to ensure accuracy and quality. Specifically, each annotated example was first completed by one annotator, then reviewed by a second annotator to verify the correctness. If disagreements or ambiguities arose, the case was escalated to a third annotator for judgment. In instances where consensus could not be reached among all three annotators, the corresponding instruction was excluded from the dataset.

Thank you again for your detailed feedback. We will include more explanation about our human filtering and annotation process.

summary.value: The paper presents OCRBench v2, an advanced benchmark designed to evaluate large multimodal models (LMMs) across a variety of text-oriented visual understanding tasks. It introduces 23 tasks within eight core competencies, including text recognition, element parsing, and knowledge reasoning. OCRBench v2 is built on 10,000 human-validated question-answer pairs and aims to assess the OCR capabilities of LMMs in real-world scenarios, filling the gap left by previous benchmarks. Notably, it provides a private test set for reliable evaluation and reveals the limitations of current models.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Comprehensive Coverage: OCRBench v2 is notable for its extensive range, covering both basic and advanced OCR tasks. The inclusion of 31 diverse scenarios and 23 tasks provides a robust platform for evaluating LMMs in real-world OCR applications.

2. High-Quality Data: The use of 10,000 high-quality, human-verified instruction-response pairs, along with a private test set, ensures rigorous evaluation and prevents overfitting, making the benchmark highly reliable.

3. Holistic Approach: The benchmark combines tasks under eight core OCR competencies, facilitating systematic comparisons of model strengths and weaknesses. It also enables deeper insights into areas where current models still fail, such as fine-grained text recognition and logical reasoning.

4. Revealing Model Limitations: The evaluation of existing LMMs identifies clear areas for improvement, including text spotting, element parsing, and complex reasoning tasks, which can guide future research in OCR-enhanced LMMs.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. I believe there is an issue with the paper. Although it covers many text-related tasks, for example, the Mathematical Reasoning task in Figure 1 actually resembles more of a Visual Math Reasoning problem, with the only difference being that the question is converted into optical characters. Is it really necessary to include such tasks in OCRBench? Similarly, the Reasoning VQA maze task in Figure 3 should not be a focus of OCRBench. It is more about evaluating the model’s logical reasoning ability. If the authors intend to include it in their benchmark, they should differentiate whether the model's failure is due to incorrect character recognition or a lack of reasoning capability, which would align better with OCRBench's purpose. Otherwise, the resulting scores and rankings may not truly reflect the OCR capabilities of the models and could mislead many in the community.

2. As a benchmark, the weighted scores across different tasks significantly affect the model's performance in the average. The paper does not seem to discuss the weights of its 23 tasks, nor which tasks accurately reflect real-world application needs and fundamental OCR abilities. Providing feedback on a model’s foundational OCR capabilities and its ability to solve practical problems is what a benchmark should focus on. This would have a more positive impact on the community, rather than getting caught up in an "arms race" to cover a wide range of tasks and pile on more features.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

final_justification.value: I buy into the authors’ argument in the Discussion that current benchmarks need a more comprehensive question-evaluation approach and that the divide between perception and cognition is not as wide. This addresses my initial concern. I am raising my score to 5.

summary.value: This work presents a large-scale bilingual, text-centric benchmark that outperforms the previous multi-scene OCRBench by offering a significantly broader range of tasks: four times more than its predecessor. The benchmark also provides the most extensive coverage of diverse scenarios, encompassing 31 distinct contexts. Additionally, it presents a comprehensive set of evaluation metrics and includes 10,000 human-verified question-answering pairs, with a notable emphasis on challenging samples. Furthermore, a private test set comprising 1,500 manually annotated images is also constructed, contributing to the robustness of the benchmark. The authors benchmarked extensive recent SOTA algorithms on the proposed dataset and the experimental results demonstrate that there is still a large room to improve.

strengths_contributions.value:
1) This paper presents a very comprehensive and extensive OCR benchmark to evaluate the MLLMs on visual text localization and reasoning. The authors constructed an improved benchmark to assess eight core OCR competencies and cover 23 tasks across 31 diverse scenarios, which provides a thorough evaluation framework encapsulating fundamental and advanced text-centric challenges.

2) The authors have considered some challenging and corner cases to evaluate the existing MLLMs. From the experimental results, there is still a large room for existing open-source and closed-source algorithms to improve. 

3) The authors provide some important findings and insights regarding the OCR task for future improvements.

limitations_weaknesses.value:

summary.value: The submission introduces OCRBench v2, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate the OCR capabilities of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) across visual text localization and reasoning tasks. It aims to address the limitations of existing benchmarks, which lack diversity and complexity, by offering 23 tasks spanning 8 core OCR capabilities—text recognition, text referring, text spotting, relation extraction, element parsing, mathematical calculation, visual text understanding, and knowledge reasoning—across 31 diverse scenarios. The benchmark includes 10,000 human-verified question-answering (QA) pairs and a private test set of 1,500 manually annotated images, supported by six tailored evaluation metrics. Through extensive testing of state-of-the-art LMMs, the authors reveal critical limitations, such as struggles with text localization and logical reasoning, and provide a publicly available benchmark and evaluation scripts. The primary contributions are a robust evaluation framework, systematic LMM performance baselines, and detailed insights into model limitations.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. OCRBench v2 expands the scope of OCR evaluation with 23 tasks across 8 core capabilities, a fourfold increase over the previous OCRBench’s 5 tasks.

2. The benchmark’s 10,000 human-verified QA pairs and 1,500-image private test set ensure high-quality, contamination-free evaluation. Consistent performance trends across public and private sets (Section 4.2) validate its reliability, making it a trustworthy tool compared to potentially contaminated datasets like DocVQA.

3. The paper clearly contrasts OCRBench v2 with existing benchmarks (e.g., OCRBench, DocVQA, TableVQA-Bench), justifying its necessity through performance saturation (e.g., 88.8% on OCRBench) and limited task diversity in predecessors.

4. The paper is well-written and organized.

limitations_weaknesses.value: 1. The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of specific cases where multiple LMMs consistently fail, limiting insights into common failure modes across models.

summary.value: This paper introduces OCRBench v2, a large-scale, bilingual benchmark designed to evaluate the Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and reasoning capabilities of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs). It addresses the limitations of existing benchmarks, which do not sufficiently explore challenging tasks like text localization, handwritten content extraction, and logical reasoning. OCRBench v2 is comprehensive, featuring 23 tasks across 31 diverse scenarios, with 10,000 human-verified question-answer pairs. To ensure a fair assessment of model generalization, the authors also constructed a private test set of 1,500 manually annotated images that will not be publicly released. Through extensive benchmarking of state-of-the-art LMMs, the study reveals that most models score below 50 out of 100 and identifies five key areas of weakness: recognition of less common text, fine-grained perception, layout perception, complex element parsing, and logical reasoning.

strengths_contributions.value:
The benchmark is extensive, encompassing 23 tasks and 31 scenarios. This is a significant expansion over previous benchmarks, such as the original OCRBench, providing a more thorough evaluation framework.

The benchmark assesses eight core text-reading abilities, from fundamental text recognition and referring to advanced knowledge reasoning and mathematical calculation. This allows for a holistic and systematic comparison of model capabilities.

The benchmark includes 10,000 high-quality, human-validated instruction-response pairs. The authors ensured data quality by manually reviewing all instructions for the public data and correcting annotation errors.

The paper establishes broad baselines by evaluating a wide range of open-source and commercial LMMs. This analysis leads to insightful findings about the common limitations of current models.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
The benchmark's design deliberately focuses only on single-image text-related scenarios. While the authors justify this as a focus on a fundamental problem, it omits the challenge of multi-page or multi-image document understanding, which is a critical aspect of many real-world applications.

The paper mentions that the benchmark construction involved human filtering and annotation, but it lacks detailed documentation regarding the specific annotation protocols, inter-annotator agreement statistics, or how ambiguous cases were resolved.

title.value: OCRBench v2: An Improved Benchmark for Evaluating Large Multimodal Models on Visual Text Localization and Reasoning

abstract.value: Scoring the Optical Character Recognition (OCR) capabilities of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) has witnessed growing interest. Existing benchmarks have highlighted the impressive performance of LMMs in text recognition; however, their abilities in certain challenging tasks, such as text localization, handwritten content extraction, and logical reasoning, remain underexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce OCRBench v2, a large-scale bilingual text-centric benchmark with currently the most comprehensive set of tasks ($4\times$ more tasks than the previous multi-scene benchmark OCRBench), the widest coverage of scenarios ($31$ diverse scenarios), and thorough evaluation metrics, with $10,000$ human-verified question-answering pairs and a high proportion of difficult samples. Moreover, we construct a private test set with $1,500$ manually annotated images. The consistent evaluation trends observed across both public and private test sets validate the OCRBench v2's reliability. After carefully benchmarking state-of-the-art LMMs, we find that most LMMs score below $50$ ($100$ in total) and suffer from five-type limitations, including less frequently encountered text recognition, fine-grained perception, layout perception, complex element parsing, and logical reasoning. The benchmark and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/Yuliang-Liu/MultimodalOCR.
